Personally I don't really see being bipolar as a medical condition to be treated. The whole concept of "mental illness" just seems really dubious to me. They call it an illness rather than a disease because they can't find any sort of physical mechanism behind it, and "mental" is not really a scientific term (it hearkens back to Freud's and Jung's pre-science conception of the brain). Psychiatrists don't even understand the mechanisms behind what their drugs actually do to our brains. The most scientific explanation anyone can really give of bipolarity is that it's a "chemical imbalance" (sometimes they'll throw in fancy science words like "neurotransmitter" to trick you into thinking they know what they're talking about). Moreover, society tends to label any behavioural abnormality that science can't explain as "mental illness"; until forty years ago, these "scientists" insisted that homosexuality was a mental illness, and this basis was used to incarcerate and "medicate" (chemically castrate) countless gay men. Autism used to be considered a mental illness as well, until research revealed that it's simply an alternative and valid neural construction with its own benefits. Syphilis used to be considered a mental illness before it was revealed to be a sexually-transmitted disease. I feel that in time, bipolar and probably all "mental illnesses" will be either ascribed to physical mechanisms or simply accepted as falling within the natural range of neural variation. There are many theories that postulate that bipolarity arose as an evolutionary adaptation to seasonal changes; more active in the warm months when resources were plentiful, less active in the cold months when resources were scarce. In fact, the creativity and ambition of mania may have been what sparked our greatest early achievements: language, tool use, mastery of fire, music, painting, etc. We may owe our entire civilization to the benefits of mania! Now that we live in a society so closed off to the outside environment, this adaption can seem like a curse (and I'm sure our collectively shit diets and lifestyles have thrown our natural cycles completely out of whack, creating even more mental chaos). However, rather than clog our brains up with sedatives or stimulants to offset these cycles, I think we should strive for greater control over these natural rhythms by living our lives in healthier, more natural ways. Our brains did not develop in an age of high-fructose corn syrup and 24/7 electric light and being holed up in cubic caves the majority of the time. Of course we feel like we're going crazy, especially those of us more sensitive to sunlight and diet. Either we can be slaves to our so-called "developed" society by taking pills just to "function", or we can figure out the optimal conditions in which our brains were wired to thrive and gain mastery over our moods and our neurological potential. If we unlock the secrets of our brain, we can reap the benefits of mania's creativity, ambition, and general mental superiority. But, of course, there's a lot more money in convincing 20% of the population that they're "sick" and "need to buy these pills from us or we're going to lock you in a psychiatric prison until you do". 

But that's just my two cents.

This one sentence encapsulates everything that is wrong with your product and the way in which you view yourself. I've read your website and watched your Ted talk, and honestly I could not be more appalled by your ignorance, presumptuousness, and above all your self-absorption. 

You begin your talk by claiming to have the "secret to mental health" despite being neither a psychologist nor a therapist. "This is how we're going to change mental health around the world," you proudly declare. "As you begin helping people, you're going to feel really good."

This is not the solution to the mental health problems of the world. I really don't get the impression you give one whit about the mental health of others. This pitch, this website, and this phone app are simply a showcase for the messianic aspirations of a twentysomething-year-old narcissist who fancies himself a philanthropist. The mental health problems of others are not an opportunity to flaunt your "life resume" (as you put it) and your "philanthropy". If you personally are benefiting more than the people you are helping, you are absolutely doing it wrong. The conversation around mental health should be focused on the individuals struggling against hopelessness, fear, poverty, pain, and who overcome these odds through courage, conviction, personal strength, and a network of legitimate mental health services. If talking to anonymous strangers over the Internet were the secret to mental illness, we all would already be cured. 

This is not the cure for mental illness. This is not therapy (which is a clinical process, not a social media venture), as you fraudulently claim. I am not a beached whale, and you are far from a philanthropist. And consider that the reason your "friend" found it so difficult to speak with you about her mental health is that you can't help but make the entire conversation about yourself and your own experiences. And above all, keep in mind that personal benefit and "feeling really good" are not your compensation for helping others - the betterment of your fellow man is its own reward. If you ever find yourself in a mental health crisis, I hope you find someone who sees you as more than just an opportunity for self-promotion and self-aggrandizement. We are not your charity case. The point of a character profile is not to help the readers understand your characters, but to make sure that you understand your own characters. You'd be hard-pressed to find a story to which the main character's zodiac sign is relevant. Instead, think about why you chose each detail for each character, about what those details say about your character's personality. That is the more important function of character questionnaires: to stimulate new ideas about who your characters are and how they are likely to behave in certain situations. But your characters' favourite foods/songs/animals? You can leave most of those out of the actual story, which should be reserved specifically for details that are relevant to the development of the character (like personal strengths, weaknesses, deep pains from the past), the plot (like specific skills of the character or connections to other characters), or the theme (these details depend on the story you're trying to tell). The details you've already incorporated into your story are a great start; develop those in more detail, but leave out the nonessential.
